objetivo: Say where in Brazil people live and come from, describe the main festivals (Carnaval, festa junina and São João, Círio de Nazaré), talk about regional food, words and accents with respect, and understand a short personal text about them.

sessoes.titulo: Regions, states and where people are from

blocos.enunciado: Say aloud: three connectors from lesson 52, one opinion with «acho que» and one with «não acho que» + subjunctive (lesson 53). Then say where you live and where you are from.

itens.pt: the interior (away from the big cities and the coast)

blocos.titulo: The five regions, states with «em / no / na» and the words for where people come from
blocos.explicacao: STEP 1: Brazil has 26 states and the Federal District (where Brasília is). They are usually grouped into five regions: Norte (for example Pará, Amazonas), Nordeste (Bahia, Pernambuco, Ceará), Centro-Oeste (Goiás, Mato Grosso), Sudeste (São Paulo, Rio de Janeiro, Minas Gerais, Espírito Santo) and Sul (Paraná, Santa Catarina, Rio Grande do Sul). Each region has big cities, small towns, coast and countryside: no region is just one thing. STEP 2: prepositions. Use «em» for a place: «em São Paulo», «em Minas Gerais», «em Pernambuco». Many states take an article, so «em» + «o/a» becomes «no/na»: «no Rio de Janeiro», «no Pará», «no Ceará», «na Bahia», «no Rio Grande do Sul». For origin use «de» (+ article): «Sou de São Paulo», «Sou do Pará», «Sou da Bahia». Note that «Rio de Janeiro» (city and state) takes the article («no Rio»), while «São Paulo» does not («em São Paulo»). STEP 3: the words for people. Add «-ense», «-ano» or a special word: «paulista» (from the state of São Paulo), «paulistano» (from the city of São Paulo), «carioca» (from the city of Rio), «fluminense» (from the state of Rio), «mineiro» (Minas Gerais), «baiano» (Bahia), «paraense» (Pará), «pernambucano» (Pernambuco), «gaúcho» (Rio Grande do Sul), «cearense» (Ceará). Region words: «nordestino», «nortista», «sulista». STEP 4: these words are written with a small letter in Portuguese, even for nationality: «brasileiro», «mineiro». Agree with gender: «ela é gaúcha». STEP 5: treat regions with curiosity, not clichés. A person from Bahia is not always «relaxed» and a person from São Paulo is not always «in a hurry»; ask people about their city and their food instead.
blocos.comparacao: English says «in Bahia» and «in Rio» with no article. Portuguese often has an article with the place, so you need the contraction: «na Bahia», «no Pará», «no Rio Grande do Sul». The nationality and the people from a place are written in lower case: «brasileiro», «baiano», unlike «Brazilian» and «Bahian» in English.

erros.motivo: Nationalities are written with a small letter in Portuguese.
The city and state of São Paulo take no article.

blocos.enunciado: Say where you live («Moro em…» or «Moro no/na…») and where you are from («Sou de/do/da…»), then name one state in each of two regions and the word for its people (for example «mineiro», «baiano»).

blocos.titulo: Describing traditions: «costumar», the impersonal «se» and time expressions
blocos.explicacao: STEP 1: Carnaval happens in the days before Lent (Quaresma), in February or March, and it ends on the Tuesday before Ash Wednesday. It is celebrated differently in each place: in Rio de Janeiro and São Paulo, samba schools parade in large avenues; in many cities there are «blocos» in the streets; in Salvador there are «trios elétricos» (trucks with live music); in Recife and Olinda people dance «frevo» and see giant puppets. STEP 2: the «festas juninas» take place in June and honor three saints: Santo Antônio (June 13), São João (June 24) and São Pedro (June 29). People dance «quadrilha», light bonfires and eat corn-based foods (pamonha, canjica, pipoca, bolo de milho) and peanut sweets (paçoca). In the Northeast, «São João» is the biggest popular festival of the year, with large celebrations in cities such as Campina Grande (Paraíba) and Caruaru (Pernambuco). STEP 3: the «Círio de Nazaré» takes place in Belém (Pará), every year on the second Sunday of October. It is a Catholic procession in honor of Nossa Senhora de Nazaré, with a very large crowd, and it is recognized as cultural heritage in Brazil and by UNESCO. Families gather for the «almoço do Círio», with dishes such as pato no tucupi. For many it is an act of faith; for others it is above all a cultural and family tradition. STEP 4: to talk about traditions, use the present for habits, «costumar» + infinitive and the impersonal «se»: «As pessoas costumam dançar quadrilha.» «Dança-se quadrilha em junho.» «Comem-se pamonhas e canjica.» (passive «se» with a plural noun takes a plural verb, lesson 49). For the past, use the imperfect: «Antigamente, as famílias se reuniam em volta da fogueira.» STEP 5: dates and months take «em» without an article: «em junho», «em outubro»; the Sunday takes the article: «no segundo domingo de outubro».
blocos.comparacao: English talks about «Carnival» as one event. In Brazil it is several traditions in different places, from big parades to small neighborhood blocos and the music of Pernambuco. And «São João» in the Northeast is not a small event: it is as important there as Carnaval is in other places.

blocos.titulo: Describing dishes and talking about words and accents with respect
blocos.explicacao: STEP 1: to describe a dish use «é feito de/com» (is made of/with), «leva» (it contains), «é servido com» (is served with), «é típico de» (is typical of) and «é conhecido por» (is known for): «A moqueca baiana é feita com peixe, dendê e leite de coco.» «O pão de queijo é típico de Minas Gerais.» Adjectives agree: «prato típico», «comida típica». STEP 2: some well-known examples. Bahia: acarajé and moqueca baiana. Espírito Santo: moqueca capixaba, made without dendê and coconut milk. Minas Gerais: pão de queijo and feijão tropeiro. Rio Grande do Sul: churrasco and chimarrão. Pará: tacacá, pato no tucupi, and açaí served in a savory way with fish and manioc flour. Northeast: tapioca, cuscuz, carne de sol, baião de dois. Everywhere: arroz com feijão. STEP 3: words change with the region. Use «chamar de» to say it: «No Rio e na Bahia chamam de aipim; no Nordeste, de macaxeira; em São Paulo, de mandioca.» Both forms are good Portuguese; none is better. STEP 4: accents (sotaques). In Rio de Janeiro, the «s» before a consonant and at the end of a word often sounds like «sh» («mesmo» sounds like «MEZH-moo»). In the interior of São Paulo, Paraná and Minas Gerais, many speakers pronounce the «r» before a consonant like the English «r» (the «r caipira»). In Rio Grande do Sul people often use «tu» with a third-person verb («tu vai») and say «bah» and «tchê». In Minas Gerais you may hear «uai» and «trem» (thing). In Pará people say «égua!» to show surprise; in the Northeast «oxente!» is common. In some regions you hear a plain «t» and «d» before «i» instead of «tch» and «dj». STEP 5: say «sotaque diferente», never «sotaque errado». Everyone has an accent, and all of them are legitimate.
blocos.comparacao: English speakers also hear differences between Texas, Boston and London. Portuguese is similar: understanding is almost always easy once you hear a few examples, and nobody expects you to copy one accent. Choose the one you hear most around you (the audio in this course uses a general, widely understood pronunciation).

blocos.titulo: A post: one table, many flavors
blocos.ru:
Uma mesa, muitos sabores

Moro em São Paulo, mas minha família é de Minas Gerais e minha esposa é da Bahia. Por isso, a nossa mesa tem sempre várias histórias. Na casa dos meus pais, o café da manhã tem pão de queijo e café coado na hora. Na casa da família dela, em Salvador, o dia começa muitas vezes com tapioca e, no almoço de domingo, serve-se moqueca feita com azeite de dendê, que dá uma cor e um sabor bem característicos.

Também mudam as palavras. Eu falo mandioca, ela fala aipim e uma tia dela, que mora em Recife, fala macaxeira. É a mesma raiz! E o sotaque? Cada um fala do seu jeito, e ninguém fala “errado”: o importante é a gente se entender e se divertir com as diferenças.
blocos.pt:
One table, many flavors

I live in São Paulo, but my family is from Minas Gerais and my wife is from Bahia. Because of that, our table always has several stories. At my parents' house, breakfast has pão de queijo and coffee strained just in time. At her family's house, in Salvador, the day often starts with tapioca and, at Sunday lunch, they serve moqueca made with dendê oil, which gives a very characteristic color and flavor.

The words change too. I say mandioca, she says aipim, and an aunt of hers, who lives in Recife, says macaxeira. It is the same root! And the accent? Each person speaks in their own way, and nobody speaks «wrong»: the important thing is that we understand each other and enjoy the differences.

perguntas.pergunta: Where does the author live, and where do his parents and his wife's family come from?
perguntas.resposta: He lives in São Paulo; his family is from Minas Gerais and his wife is from Bahia (her family lives in Salvador).

perguntas.pergunta: What does breakfast include at his parents' house?
perguntas.resposta: Pão de queijo and freshly strained coffee.

perguntas.pergunta: What does dendê give to the moqueca?
Which three words does the text give for the same root, and who uses each?
perguntas.resposta: Mandioca (the author), aipim (his wife), macaxeira (her aunt in Recife).

perguntas.pergunta: What is the author's attitude toward different accents?
perguntas.resposta: Nobody speaks «wrong»; the important thing is to understand each other and enjoy the differences.

Say aloud: where you live and where you are from, one festival with its month and place, one regional dish with «é feito com», and one sentence about accents with «diferente».

blocos.enunciado: Tell a friend about a Brazilian festival or dish you would like to know. Say where it is, when it is, what people do or eat, and end with a respectful remark about regional differences.

notasParaOAluno: You can now name the regions and states with the right prepositions, describe traditions with «costumar» and the impersonal «se», talk about regional dishes and words, and treat accents as variety, not error. Next lesson: living in Brazil (bank, CPF, SUS, Pix and documents).
